    t=g['text']; ch=[]

        if v is None or c is None: continue
        ok=abs(v-c)<1e-6
        ch.append((m,e,c,v,ok))

    out=[];stop=None;bad=None

agent_explanations_oldest_first.text: Mean logprob per text moved only slightly, and mostly downward, but that average includes prompt tokens. The real test is the token-class comparison. I'll write one reusable comparison function that returns paired per-text differences with standard errors for each class: first digit of retrieved numbers, later digits, result digits, plus answer-word tokens. It will also report first-break counts and the loop-probe outcome. I'll reuse the same function for every screened candidate, so they can all be compared directly. If `fromproblem` first digits improve with no cost elsewhere, the head's gain is causal.

The causal test gave a negative result for E2. Boosting the retrieval head by 1.5 left `fromproblem_first` accuracy unchanged (-0.13 ± 0.17 points) and slightly hurt result digits (-0.5 points). So this head isn't limited by its output share. When retrieval fails, it probably points to the wrong place rather than being too weak, and scaling can't fix that. The correlation I saw was real but not a lever. I'm dropping E2. Next I want to widen the search with two free text analyses. First, `othernum` is the second-biggest break class, so I'll check whether it's mainly number words ("three", "twice", "half", "dozen") that a digit-oriented retrieval circuit could miss, and how much accuracy differs. Second, Here versus Let didn't matter, but the reference solutions use a different plain-sentence style that often opens with "First". I'll look at which alternative openers the model gives non-trivial probability, and at the share of reference openers, to judge whether a third style could be worth testing. A clear weakness on number words would be a specific new circuit target, while a viable third opener would be worth one generation pass.

Number words aren't the weakness: they're retrieved at 0.776, the same as digits. The weak `othernum` subclasses are derived quantities (0.582) and unit constants (0.587), which are implicit mental arithmetic. A third opener doesn't look natural either: "Okay" has 0.05% probability and everything else is around 1e-5, so forcing one would be a large push that repairs no identified failure. I'll set that aside. A more useful idea came out of the E2 result: boosting the retrieval head hurt result digits, which suggests attention affects arithmetic and that heads compete there. Arithmetic also matters more than the crude bound implied, because a per-step error compounds across about 3.3 steps. If per-step accuracy rose from 88% to 95%, solved problems would increase by about 29%, which is roughly +5 points. So I'll analyse arithmetic the way I analysed retrieval: from the same stored attention data, I'll find which heads attend to the operands when predicting result digits, separately for first and later digits, with the share landing on the correct operands. I'll also recompute the true per-equation error rates per operator, deduplicated and on finished answers only. If a specific head attends to operands at result tokens, that's the next circuit to test.

This is the sharpest finding yet, in two parts. First, layer 17 contains a separate operand circuit: at result digits, heads h2 and h3 put 0.59-0.62 of their attention on the equation's operands with peak hit rates of 0.76-0.85, and h1 does the same for first digits only. So L17 h0 retrieves numbers from the problem, while h1-h3 read the operands. That also explains why boosting h0 hurt result digits: the output is RMS-normalised, so its boost took share from the operand heads. Second, arithmetic error isn't uniform at all. It's 3% for small two-factor products and 11% for small two-term sums, but 25-70% for three-term sums and 79% for four-term sums. Long sums are a specific failure, and they tend to be the final step that sets the answer. The operand heads might be covering only some of the terms. Three things come next. I'll check whether wrong sums equal a partial sum of the terms, which would show dropped operands. I'll build an arithmetic screening set from the model's own contexts, with corrected results, so I can measure each operator and term-count class. Then I'll run a new baseline on that set, because future edits need a paired reference. If wrong sums often equal partial sums, then operand coverage is the mechanism and attention-based edits have a clear target.
